lead: Kansas homes face hail, tornadoes, flash floods and hard freezes. DryFlare helps owners from Wichita to Overland Park get water out and get drying started.
risk: hail and wind damage, flash floods and frozen pipes
why: Kansas has had 43 severe storm disasters since 2000, more than almost any state. Large hail cracks shingles and skylights, and leaks show up later. Tornadoes like the one that leveled Greensburg in 2007 open whole roofs to the rain. Flash floods hit the Kansas City suburbs when heavy storms stall.

Winter cold is the other half. Arctic air can drop temperatures below zero in a day, and pipes in outside walls and garages freeze. Many Kansas homes have basements, so a burst pipe or failed sump pump fills them fast. Missouri and Oklahoma share the same storm track.
image_alt: Roof and window damage after a severe hail and wind storm
image_caption: Hail-cracked shingles and broken windows let rain inside long after a Kansas storm passes.
problems: Wichita, Johnson County and western Kansas
Kansas City metro creeks and low streets
Garages, crawl spaces and outside walls
tips: After hail, get the roof inspected even if nothing leaks yet.
Know where your water shut-off is and test it once a year.
Keep the garage door closed in cold weather if pipes run through it.
Clean gutters before spring storm season.
insurance: Many Kansas policies carry a separate wind and hail deductible, often a percentage of the home's insured value.

faq.q: How soon should I report hail damage in Kansas?
faq.a: As soon as you can. Many policies require prompt notice and set time limits for roof claims. Take photos, cover openings to stop more damage, and keep receipts for tarps and emergency repairs.
